Cooperation Without Adaptation: LLM Agents in a Collective-Risk Dilemma

CCS: Computing methodologies Multi-agent systems

Abstract.

Language-model agents are increasingly deployed to act on behalf of people in settings where individual decisions shape shared outcomes. We examine whether five production models adapt their contributions to changing risks and partner behaviour, or instead follow a relatively fixed strategy. In a collective-risk dilemma game (CRG), six players contribute to a shared pool over ten rounds; if the pool falls short of its target, a catastrophe may destroy their remaining resources. Four models contributed approximately an equal share at every positive risk level, and four of the five also contributed when risk was zero, even though contributing could not improve their payoff. Explicitly stating that only the agent’s own payoff mattered reduced zero-risk contributions for most models, while a more neutral prompt did not. Several models correctly identified which action offered the higher expected payoff at different risk levels, yet their contributions changed little. Against fixed partners, no model consistently chose the payoff-maximising response, and in mixed-model groups, a single agent’s shortfall in the final round could cause an otherwise successful group to fail. Payoff-based selection also depended on population composition: in a single six-agent group, it favoured the model that contributed least and reduced group success, whereas in larger, randomly mixed populations, it favoured an exact fair-share model at moderate and high risk. These findings show that cooperative self-play alone is not evidence of strategic adaptability. Consistent with a machine-behaviour approach, evaluations of agents in multi-agent systems should test how they respond to incentives, partner actions, and population composition.

Keywords: 
LLM agents, collective-risk social dilemma, cooperation, best response, empirical game-theoretic analysis, multiagent evaluation

1. Introduction

Language-model agents increasingly act on behalf of people in settings where multiple agents jointly shape a shared outcome, such as budget allocation, shared compute use, or negotiations over common resources (Chan et al., 2024; Hammond et al., 2025). These systems are therefore not only engineering artifacts: their behaviour in interactive settings is also an object of empirical study, as emphasized by the emerging field of machine behaviour (Rahwan et al., 2019). In many such settings, avoiding collective loss requires agents to incur individual costs for the benefit of the group (Santos and Pacheco, 2011; Santos et al., 2019; Milinski et al., 2008). This raises a central question for multi-agent systems (MAS) research: do language-model agents condition their cooperative behaviour on the strategic environment, or do they rely on relatively fixed behavioural defaults? From a system-design and machine-behaviour perspective, this question has three components. First, is an agent’s cooperation sensitive to the magnitude of collective risk? Second, does it respond to the behaviour of other agents in the group? Third, under selection pressures that retain or replicate higher-earning agents, which behavioural tendencies are favoured?

Success in self-play, a common criterion in MAS benchmarks (Piatti et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025), does not by itself answer these questions. When all positions in a group are occupied by copies of the same model, an agent that conditions its decisions on the stakes may generate the same observed pattern of play as an agent that follows a fixed rule. A machine-behaviour approach therefore calls for testing agents across systematically varied environments, rather than inferring their decision policies from a single setting. Success rates likewise obscure the extent to which a group falls short of the attainable optimum: a group may achieve the collective target while still dissipating a substantial share of its endowment. Moreover, a prompt that specifies both a group target and a fixed number of rounds may implicitly suggest an equal division of the burden, causing agents that simply reproduce this split to appear cooperative under conventional summary measures.

We study these questions using the collective-risk social dilemma game (CRG), a game introduced to study collective decision making for climate change mitigation (Milinski et al., 2008). Players contribute into a shared pool over several rounds, and if the pool misses a target, they all lose their savings with probability pp (Figure 1a). For risk-neutral players, group welfare is maximised when no one contributes if p<12p<\tfrac{1}{2}, and when the group meets the target exactly if p>12p>\tfrac{1}{2}, for example through the fair share, defined as an equal split of the target. The game also contains two situations in which contributing cannot raise a player’s own payoff: when there is no risk, and once the outcome is settled. Neither risk attitude nor concern for the group can explain contribution in these situations, so they separate a default from a response to the stakes.

We introduce a game-theoretic evaluation that separates cooperative outcomes from incentive-sensitive behaviour by combining risk variation, dominated-action tests, exact best responses to fixed partners and selection in mixed populations, where each model is a strategy of an empirical game (Wellman, 2006; Tuyls et al., 2018). We apply it to five production models, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, GPT-5.6 Luna, Qwen3-235B and Grok 4.20, in four designs (Figure 1b), each compared with a benchmark computed from the game. We use standard equilibrium and finite-population tools, not a new solution concept. We call near-flat contribution across risk levels under a fixed prompt a default; the term describes behaviour, not internal reasoning.

We organise our findings around three dimensions. (1) Stakes. Most models contribute roughly the fair share at every positive risk level, even when there is no risk. Removing normative wording does not change this pattern. Stating that only the agent’s own payoff matters reduces most zero-risk contributions, but only GPT-5.6 Luna shifts from contributing little at low risk to contributing the fair share at high risk. Asked in separate calls, several models rank the two choices correctly and change that ranking with the risk, but they keep contributing the same amount (Section 4.1). (2) Partners. Beside scripted partners who make every contribution a loss, no model plays the best response of contributing nothing, and two keep contributing after the outcome is already settled. In a mixed game (also referred to as a table or group), a single partner that stops contributing in the last round often causes a table of exact fair-share players to fail, while a table that overpays can absorb the shortfall. (Section 4.2). (3) Selection. Population size changes who is selected under payoff-based imitation: a population of one table favours the smallest contributor and lowers group success, whereas a larger randomly mixed population favours the exact fair-share player at moderate and high risk (Section 4.3).

2. Related work

Collective risk and selection.

The collective-risk dilemma was introduced to study why groups fail to avoid a shared disaster, and human groups reach the target mostly when the risk is high (Milinski et al., 2008); inequality and communication change how often they succeed (Tavoni et al., 2011). Threshold public goods games have many equilibria (Palfrey and Rosenthal, 1984), contributions decline over the rounds of repeated public goods games (Andreoni, 1988), and the risk of collective failure can turn a defection trap into a coordination problem (Santos and Pacheco, 2011; Merhej et al., 2021). In evolutionary simulations of the same game, constant fair sharers lose out to players who hold back early and compensate later (Abou Chakra and Traulsen, 2012). Selection on payoff relative to a small group favours whoever does better than its neighbours (Schaffer, 1988), while selection between groups can favour cooperation (Traulsen and Nowak, 2006). Finite-population analyses price the incentives that sustain cooperation in this game (Duong et al., 2026) and show that maximising cooperation need not maximise welfare (Han et al., 2024). This literature predicts that behaviour should vary with risk, so the absence of such variation is informative; we use a similar game theoretical approach to analyse how different agent types perform when placed together in mixed groups/tables.

Language models as strategic players.

Language models have been studied as economic subjects (Filippas et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023; Mei et al., 2024) and in repeated and multi-player games (Fan et al., 2024; Akata et al., 2025; Fontana et al., 2025; Pal et al., 2026; Kempinski et al., 2025; Pham et al., 2026). Models tend to be more cooperative than people (Mei et al., 2024), and an even split can reflect a focal point rather than fairness (Dodivers and Rafai, 2025). The weight of framing relative to game structure differs by model (Lorè and Heydari, 2024), and models can hold a correct belief or plan and act against it (Fan et al., 2024; Schmied et al., 2026). FAIRGAME runs language-model agents through standard games and finds outcomes that depend on model, language and persona (Buscemi et al., 2025b); later work extends it to a payoff-scaled prisoner’s dilemma and a multi-player public goods game (Huynh et al., 2025).

Language models in social dilemmas.

Societies of agents over-use a common resource (Piatti et al., 2024), contributions to a public good can stay the same even when it returns nothing (Huang et al., 2025), and reasoning models free-ride (Guzman Piedrahita et al., 2025). Agents stand in for people in a collective-risk game (Slumbers et al., 2025) and for developers, regulators and users in an evolutionary model of AI regulation (Buscemi et al., 2025a). A study of 35 open models includes a collective-risk game at one risk level and observes their decisions far from the group optimum (Kumar et al., 2026). In a binary collective-risk game with strategies written by three models, payoff-biased imitation drives larger groups to selfish, low-welfare outcomes (Willis et al., 2026), and prompts that evolve under individual selection collapse into defection while group selection keeps them prosocial (Celiktemel et al., 2026). A recent study audits rule recall, state tracking and payoff calculation before interpreting play in multi-player races to develop AI (Pham et al., 2026). It compares play with an evolutionary benchmark and human data, and finds that correct recall can coexist with weak expected-payoff calculation. We differ in three ways: we vary the risk from zero to certainty and add two tests in which contributing cannot raise the contributor’s cash; we compute the exact best response to fixed partners; and we select among deployed models with payoffs from their real mixed tables, finding that at moderate and high risk the favoured model changes once the population exceeds one table.

Multiagent evaluation.

Multiagent reinforcement learning studies cooperation in sequential social dilemmas (Leibo et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2018), and ad hoc teamwork and cooperative AI ask for agents that work with partners unlike themselves (Stone et al., 2010; Dafoe et al., 2020; Leibo et al., 2021). Empirical game-theoretic analysis treats trained agents as strategies of a meta-game (Wellman, 2006; Tuyls et al., 2018), α\alpha-Rank ranks them by evolutionary dynamics (Omidshafiei et al., 2019), and evolutionary game theory is used to study emergent behaviour in multiagent systems (Han, 2022). Language models show distinct strategic fingerprints in tournaments with classic strategies (Payne and Alloui-Cros, 2025), their cooperation evolves differently across base models (Vallinder and Hughes, 2025), and cooperation sustained by repetition weakens when co-players differ (Tewolde et al., 2026). In the collective-risk game, people who delegate to artificial agents succeed more often (Fernández Domingos et al., 2022), and in theory adaptive players compensate for the effort of artificial agents (Terrucha et al., 2024). We add a multiplayer dilemma with exact best responses to fixed partners, and measure this compensation in real models.

3. Game and evaluation design

3.1. Collective-risk game and benchmarks

Six players each start with e=40e=40 units, and the game lasts R=10R=10 rounds. In each round every player privately chooses a contribution ait∈{0,2,4}a_{i}^{t}\in\{0,2,4\} to a shared pool, and after each round all players see what every seat has contributed. Let xi=∑taitx_{i}=\sum_{t}a_{i}^{t} be a player’s total and X=∑ixiX=\sum_{i}x_{i} the pool. The target is T=120T=120. A player keeps what it did not contribute, but if the pool misses the target, a catastrophe destroys all savings with probability pp (Table 1 lists the terms used):

Proposition 3.1.

Consider the expected-payoff formulation of the game in which each player picks a total xi∈{0,2,…,40}x_{i}\in\{0,2,\dots,40\}, and let p<1p<1. A profile is a Nash equilibrium if and only if x=0x=0, or X=TX=T and xi≤p×ex_{i}\leq p\times e for every ii. A target-reaching equilibrium exists if and only if p≥p∗=T/(6​e)=12p\geq p^{*}=T/(6e)=\tfrac{1}{2}. The welfare-optimal outcome is x=0x=0 for p<p∗p<p^{*} and X=TX=T for p>p∗p>p^{*}, and both are optimal at p=p∗p=p^{*}, so the welfare-optimal mean payoff per player is opt⁡(p)=max⁡{(1−p)​e,e−T/6}\mathrm{opt}(p)=\max\{(1-p)e,\;e-T/6\}; this welfare statement also holds at p=1p=1.

Proof sketch. If X<TX<T, any player with xi>0x_{i}>0 gains by contributing nothing, so the only equilibrium that misses the target is x=0x=0. If X>TX>T, then X≥T+2X\geq T+2 because totals are even, so a player can contribute 2 less and still reach the target. If X=TX=T, the best deviation is to contribute nothing, worth (1−p)​e(1-p)e against e−xie-x_{i}, which gives xi≤p​ex_{i}\leq pe; summing over players gives p≥T/(6​e)p\geq T/(6e), and conversely xi=20x_{i}=20 for every ii is an equilibrium when p≥12p\geq\tfrac{1}{2}. Welfare is 6​e−X6e-X when the target is met and (1−p)​(6​e−X)(1-p)(6e-X) otherwise, so it peaks at X=TX=T or X=0X=0. The ten-round game, in which strategies can react to the history, has the same totals in pure-strategy Nash equilibrium (see Supplementary Material, Proposition S1, Section S2.3, for the full proof). We claim nothing about subgame perfection, and opt⁡(p)\mathrm{opt}(p) is a welfare bound that does not depend on the equilibrium concept. □\square

Proposition 3.1 gives a symmetric welfare benchmark: contribute nothing below the pivot and, above it, contribute the fair share needed to reach the threshold. Asymmetric allocations that reach exactly TT achieve the same group welfare. This benchmark is neither a unique equilibrium nor a prediction of individual play: contributing nothing is also an equilibrium at every risk level. Moreover, contributing a positive amount is strictly dominated in own expected payoff when p=0p=0 and, for p<1p<1, once the outcome is settled. These comparisons require neither risk neutrality nor beliefs about partners.

Proposition 3.2.

For two seats ii and jj in the same game, the difference in their expected payoffs over the lottery is c⁡(xj−xi)c\,(x_{j}-x_{i}), with c=1c=1 if the target was reached and c=1−pc=1-p otherwise.

Both seats face the same pool and the same lottery, so only their own contributions differ. Hence, for p<1p<1, whoever contributes less at a table earns more, whatever the group achieves.

3.2. Models, protocol and measures

We test the five models of Section 1: one production model per provider, chosen to reflect the kind of model plausibly used for deploying many agents at scale. Qwen3-235B is the instruction-tuned build without a thinking mode, and Grok 4.20 is its non-reasoning variant.

Prompts.

In each round a seat receives a prompt with the rules, the full history of every seat’s contributions, and a request for making a contribution; the Supplementary Material provides every prompt word for word (Section S4). The base prompt calls the pool a “climate account”, says that the group “must” reach the target, calls the loss a “disaster” and names the game as a collective-risk social dilemma. It never states the player’s goal, and it hints at the equal split twice. The prompt controls in Section 3.3 change exactly these parts.

Protocol.

The running pool is not shown, so any seat that needs it must compute it from the history. The prompt is in English and no seat is assigned a persona. We parse the move from the reply’s final CONTRIBUTION: line.

Measures.

We report expected payoffs, the average a seat would earn if the catastrophe lottery were run many times on the same contribution, and the share of opt⁡(p)\mathrm{opt}(p) that is lost. Proposition 3.1, opt⁡(p)\mathrm{opt}(p) and the selection fitness below all use expected payoffs, which remove the lottery noise without bias; agents never see the draw, and the Supplementary Material lists the realised draws (Table S6). The unit of analysis is the game, since seats in one game share a history and a lottery. Intervals are 95% percentile bootstraps over games and tests are permutation tests over games; Supplementary Material gives every value behind the statements below (Sections S6–S12).

3.3. Evaluation designs

Table 2 summarises the experimental designs, elaborated below; each model plays the same number of games in every design.

Self-play and prompt controls.

Six copies of one model play the base prompt at 11 risk levels p=0,0.1,…,1p=0,0.1,\dots,1, and again under prompt and decoding controls at fewer risk levels. No hint deletes the two equal-split phrases. Neutral wording replaces the normative and naming phrases with plain ones, such as “a shared account”. Goal stated keeps the neutral wording and adds an opening saying the player is in a paid experiment where “the only thing that matters to you is your own final cash payoff”. Two rewordings change the phrasing but keep every rule and the hint, one condition sets the temperature to zero, and a rerun repeats the base prompt with value questions.

Value questions.

In the rerun, separate calls whose answers never enter the game ask the first seat at the start, middle and end of the game which of two whole-game strategies gives the higher average payoff: contributing 2 in every round and reaching the target, or contributing nothing and missing it. The correct answer switches at p∗p^{*} (Supplementary Material, Section S8).

Fixed partners.

One model plays with five scripted partners of the same type. They always contribute 0, always contribute 2, always contribute 4, or copy the group, which means contributing 2 in the first round and then the allowed amount nearest to the average of what the other seats contributed in the previous round. The model is not informed that its partners are scripted, but their moves are included in the history. We compute the best response to each type, i.e. the play that earns the most, by enumerating every possible sequence of the model’s own ten moves. With partners who always contribute 0, the target cannot be reached; with partners who always contribute 4, the target is reached without the model. The best response to both is to contribute nothing, and once the history settles the outcome, contributing cannot improve the outcome and only reduces payoff. Against fair-share partners, the best response is to contribute nothing below p∗p^{*} and exactly the fair share above it; partners who copy the group never deviate from 2, thus resulting in the same best response.

Mixed tables.

To mix defaults at a table, we seat every pair of models together, with one to five seats for the first model and the rest for the second, at low, moderate and high risk. Each model’s seats form one block, fixed within a cell and alternating across cells, so every model occupies every seat equally often overall.

Selection among models.

We finally examine which model prevails under payoff-based retention or imitation, and how this outcome depends on population size. We treat each LLM as a strategy in an empirical game, i.e. using experimentally estimated payoffs from model interactions to define the game (Wellman, 2006; Tuyls et al., 2018). We write πA​(k)\pi_{A}(k) for the mean expected payoff of an AA seat at a table with kk seats of AA and 6−k6-k of BB, from mixed tables for 1≤k≤51\leq k\leq 5 and from self-play (grid plus rerun) for k=6k=6. A population of NN agents consists of ii agents of type AA and N−iN-i of type BB, and each agent’s five tablemates are drawn at random from the other N−1N-1, as in e.g.  (Santos and Pacheco, 2011; Han et al., 2017; Santos et al., 2020). The fitness of each type is its payoff averaged over the tables/interactions it participates in:

(2) fA​(i)\displaystyle f_{A}(i) =∑k=16ℋ⁡(k−1,N−1,i−1)​πA​(k),\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{6}\mathcal{H}(k-1;\,N-1,\,i-1)\;\pi_{A}(k),
fB​(i)\displaystyle f_{B}(i) =∑k=05ℋ⁡(k,N−1,i)​πB​(6−k),\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{k=0}^{5}\mathcal{H}(k;\,N-1,\,i)\;\pi_{B}(6-k),

where ℋ⁡(k,N−1,m)\mathcal{H}(k;\,N-1,\,m) is the hypergeometric chance that kk of five tablemates come from the mm other agents of type AA. Under Fermi imitation (Traulsen et al., 2006; Han et al., 2017), a randomly selected agent copies a random other agent’s strategy with probability 1/(1+e−β​Δ​f)1/(1+e^{-\beta\Delta f}), where Δ​f\Delta f is the other’s fitness minus its own and β=1\beta=1 per payoff unit. We assume rare mutation (Fudenberg and Imhof, 2006; Han et al., 2017), which has been shown to provide a strong approximation beyond the strict rare-mutation regime (Han et al., 2012; Rand et al., 2013; Zisis et al., 2015; Sigmund et al., 2010): each newcomer either fixes or disappears before the next arrives. Pairwise fixation probabilities then define a Markov chain over the five homogeneous model populations. Its stationary mass gives each model’s long-run weight, and EGTtools (Fernández Domingos et al., 2023) was used to reproduce the fixation probabilities and stationary distributions of Figure 5. With N=6N=6 the whole population is one table; with N=30N=30, fitness averages over random, overlapping tables. Changing NN changes both table compositions and fixation dynamics, not only whom an agent is compared with. We evaluate this finite-population process, not a scoring-only intervention.

4. Results

4.1. Stakes: contribution does not scale with risk

4.1.1. Self-play across risk

Four of the five models contribute approximately the fair share at every positive risk level (Figure 2a). Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, GPT-5.6 Luna and Qwen3-235B contribute almost the same amount below the pivot as above it (a step of at most 0.2 units), whereas the symmetric welfare benchmark jumps from contributing nothing to the fair share. In the original experiment with the same rules, human groups reached the target in half of their games at p=0.9p=0.9 and in none at p=0.1p=0.1  (Milinski et al., 2008). Strong risk aversion could explain a flat contribution profile above zero risk: because catastrophe leaves players with nothing, a player with relative risk aversion near one may prefer a certain fair-share contribution even at low risk. Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite provides the clearest example. Almost every seat plays the exact split at every risk level (Table 3), so this near-fixed rule attains the welfare optimum above the pivot but not below it.

Paying when there is nothing to protect.

Four of the five models also contribute at p=0p=0, about as much as at any other risk level (Table 3, first column). Contributing there only lowers a player’s own payoff and helps nobody, so neither risk attitude nor concern for others’ payoff can explain this contribution. GPT-5.6 Luna is the exception. It contributes nothing at p=0p=0 and its usual share at every positive risk, so it distinguishes zero risk from positive risk but does not respond to how high the risk is.

Three ways to lose.

The models lose payoff in three different ways (Table 3, Figure 2c). Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna lose mostly at low risk, where they contribute for a target that is not worth reaching. Grok 4.20 overpays: its groups reach the target well before the last round, and its seats keep contributing into a pool that is already safe. Qwen3-235B fails at the end. It contributes 2 round after round, then almost all of its seats contribute nothing in the last round (Figure 2b). Its groups therefore almost never reach the target, although every one of them would have succeeded had each seat simply repeated its previous move. Success rates hide all of this. Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and Grok 4.20 both reach the target in every game, yet Grok 4.20 keeps far less of its endowment . For 0.5<p<10.5<p<1, Qwen3-235B and Grok 4.20 groups earn less in most games than in the worst equilibrium of Proposition 3.1, in which nobody contributes. In the last round, Qwen3-235B skips as often when its contribution is needed as when the others’ fair shares already suffice, so its skip follows the round number rather than the pool; human contributions similarly decline over the rounds of repeated public goods games (Andreoni, 1988). GPT-5.6 Luna skips mostly when its contribution is not needed, and Claude Haiku 4.5 stops mostly once the target is reached (Supplementary Material, Section S12.1).

4.1.2. Prompt and objective controls

The default effect persists under rewording, but the resulting failures do not.

Deleting the two equal-split phrases does not reduce any model’s contribution (Table 4), indicating that the hint was not the source of contributions. Instead, it bounded contributions for some models while enabling others contribute exactly 2 per round. Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite still plays the exact split, which it can rebuild from the target, while GPT-5.6 Luna keeps its average contribution but plays the exact split less often. Qwen3-235B and Grok 4.20 contribute more without the hint; Qwen3-235B now reaches the target, but it earns less because it overpays. The two rewordings and a temperature of zero leave the contributions of the four models other than Grok 4.20 almost unchanged. The failures are less stable than the averages. Under the second rewording Grok 4.20 contributes about the fair share, and how often Qwen3-235B drops out in the last round varies widely across prompts. Grok 4.20’s rise with risk on the grid recurs at temperature zero but not in the rerun or the second rewording, so we do not interpret it as a stable response.

Stating the goal, not removing norms, reduces zero-risk contributions.

The normative words are not the main source of the default. With neutral wording, most models still contribute at p=0p=0. At low and high risk the four models other than Grok 4.20 contribute on average what they contributed before, while Grok 4.20 contributes even more and GPT-5.6 Luna plays the exact split less often (Table 4). Adding the stated goal is what changes play at zero risk: Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite then contribute almost nothing, Qwen3-235B contributes far less than before, and Grok 4.20 barely changes. The goal still does not make most models weigh the risk. Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite now separate zero from positive risk but already contribute the fair share at low risk, a pattern that strong risk aversion could also produce. Only GPT-5.6 Luna changes from contributing little at low risk to the fair share at high risk. Qwen3-235B contributes slightly more at high than at low risk but less than before at every risk level, and never reaches the target; Grok 4.20 still overpays.

For most models, behaviour at zero risk changes depending on whether the prompt clearly states the goal. When risk above zero, models tend to contribute similar amounts across risk levels, and this pattern remains under different wordings. The partner and selection results below use the base prompt.

Correct answers, unchanged play.

Asked the value question in separate calls, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and GPT-5.6 Luna mostly answer correctly and change their answer with the risk, yet the questioned seats contribute almost the same at low and high risk; Qwen3-235B and Grok 4.20 mostly answer that keeping pays more. This is a gap between answers and play, not evidence about what an agent computes; the Supplementary Material gives every answer and the answers against play (Section S8.6). A strongly risk-averse agent could give these answers and still contribute; contribution at p=0p=0 and after settlement provides the sharper test.

4.2. Partners: simple responses, unstable play

4.2.1. Fixed partners

No model keeps all its endowment when that is the best response.

The model contributes nothing only when paired with partners who always contribute either 0 or 4. Of the 1,000 scripted games, only 186 are played exactly optimally, and in every case the optimum is the fair share. In other words, the models reach the optimum only when it coincides with the default contribution. Since an agent unaware that its partners are scripted may reasonably contribute early to learn their behaviour, the cleaner evidence comes from contributions made after the outcome has settled (Table 5).

Partners matter, risk does not.

We split the variation in what a model contributes across games with three fixed-amount partners into partner, risk and interaction parts. For Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, GPT-5.6 Luna and Qwen3-235B, partner type explains most of the variation (69% to 92%), while risk and its interaction with partner type explain at most 5%. For an exact best responder in the same games, risk would explain half of the variation. Beside fair-share partners, where the best response jumps from nothing to the fair share at p∗p^{*}, no model’s total contribution changes by more than 2 between the low- and high-risk conditions. Grok 4.20’s total follows neither pattern: it is driven largely by its opening move, which is its largest contribution in around half of its games.

Responses to partners take simple forms.

The models adjust their contributions in response to their partners, but not in the way a best responder would (Table 5; Figures S4 and S5 of the Supplementary Material show every round). Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite contributes its usual amount, while both it and Claude Haiku 4.5 stop contributing once the history indicates that the outcome is settled. With partners who always contribute 4, GPT-5.6 Luna contributes little even when the outcome is settled, remaining close to a best response as it learns its partners’ behaviour. Qwen3-235B contributes more, not less, when interacting with partners who contribute nothing. Both Qwen3-235B and Grok 4.20 also continue making large contributions after the outcome is settled – a behaviour that no belief about their partners can justify. Against five fair-share partners, Qwen3-235B contributes 2 for nine rounds and then nothing, so the table misses the target in almost every game by that single payment; Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite in the same seat reaches it every time.

4.2.2. Mixed tables

At a shared table every model earns more than Grok 4.20, while the payoff differences among the other four models are small (Figure 3, above the diagonal). This is consistent with Proposition 3.2: Grok 4.20 contributes the most, and at a two-model table the higher contributor earns less. Group success depends on the pair (Figure 3, below the diagonal). Tables that include Grok 4.20 reach the target in the great majority of games, while tables that mix Qwen3-235B with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite or GPT-5.6 Luna rarely do.

An exact fair-share target leaves no margin for error.

One partner who stops contributing in the final round can cause a table of fair-share players to fail (Figure 4a). When the pool is one round of fair shares short before the last round, Qwen3-235B contributes nothing in 92% of cases and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite in 0.1%. Five Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite seats with one Qwen3-235B seat succeed in only 11 of 30 games, although Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite alone never misses in our sample; tables with GPT-5.6 Luna also succeed less often. Tables of Claude Haiku 4.5 or Grok 4.20, which contribute more, absorb the same partner. Replacing all Qwen3-235B last-round zeros by 2, holding other recorded actions fixed, would rescue 92% of the 323 failed mixed tables containing it. This is an arithmetic counterfactual, not a tested intervention. Conversely, one Grok 4.20 seat helps five Qwen3-235B seats succeed in most games, contributing for the rescue. These comparisons depend on the base prompt and the fixed seat blocks.

Agents free-ride on generous partners.

Most agents contribute less as the number of Grok 4.20 seats increases from one to five (Figure 4b). Alongside five Grok 4.20 seats, GPT-5.6 Luna contributes 10.5 units, and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and Claude Haiku 4.5 also fall below the fair share; these two stop once the pool reaches the target, while GPT-5.6 Luna contributes less from the start. Qwen3-235B does not show this decline. Within a cell, Grok 4.20’s higher opening contributions are associated with lower total contributions by Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and Claude Haiku 4.5, mainly through earlier target completion. GPT-5.6 Luna also contributes less while the pool is short, consistent with the compensation predicted alongside artificial agents (Terrucha et al., 2024). Openings are not randomised and partners can react to a deviation, so this association identifies neither a causal response nor an exact best response.

4.3. Selection: population-size dependent

In a one-table population, selection favours the model that contributes least. Proposition 3.2 explains why: within a game, contributing less leads to a higher individual payoff relative to the other players. In our data, Qwen3-235B contributes least relative to its tablemates, so selection gives it the greatest weight (Figure 5a). But this individual advantage comes at a cost to the group: tables reach the target less often when models are selected this way than when a model is chosen uniformly at random. At p=0.9p=0.9, for example, the target is reached in 47% of selected games, compared with 76% of randomly selected games. This illustrates the known result that selection based on payoffs relative to a small group favours whoever does better than its neighbours, even when this comes at a cost to the group (Schaffer, 1988). Here, we observe this dynamic in games played by deployed language models.

In larger populations, selection favours Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite at moderate and high risk (Figure 5b). Its self-play attains the welfare optimum there, but neither optimality nor Nash equilibrium implies that imitation will select it. The ranking comes from the estimated payoffs at every composition along the fixation path, where a lower contributor can earn more than its tablemates even while lowering its own payoff (Figure 5c, d). At low risk both population sizes favour Qwen3-235B, whose outcome remains far below the optimum. The switch to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite occurs already at seven or eight agents, consistent with finite-population theory (Schaffer, 1988).

Each winner is stable under bootstrap resampling, stronger selection, larger NN and grid-only payoffs, but not under weak selection or when a candidate is removed (Supplementary Material, Sections S11.4 and S11.6).

5. Conclusion and discussion

Our results have shown that cooperative-looking self-play is not sufficient evidence that an agent responds appropriately to incentives or adapts to its partners. Across the five models, contributions often remain close to the fair share as risk changes, including when contributing is payoff-dominated; some models also contribute after their actions can no longer affect the outcome. In mixed tables, one late shortfall can make an exact fair-share target fail. Selection outcomes depend on population structure: in a one-table population, selection can favour the lowest contributor at the group’s expense, while larger randomly mixed populations favour the fair-share model at moderate and high risk.

These findings matter for how we understand machine behaviour. A cooperative action need not reflect a stable preference for cooperation or an understanding of its consequences: it may instead be a default response to the prompt or a learned focal-point strategy. This empirical approach to auditing agent behaviour—treating models as subjects for observation in varied, interactive environments—aligns with the call to systematically study machine behaviour (Rahwan et al., 2019). Conversely, correctly identifying the payoff-maximising action when asked does not ensure that a model will choose it in play. We therefore distinguish what models can state from how they behave, and caution against treating self-play success as evidence of strategic competence, social preference, or reliable adaptation. Evaluations should vary incentives and partner behaviour, test mixed populations, and compare individual payoffs with group welfare. They should also report the welfare benchmark, identify dominated actions, and measure contributions after the outcome is settled. This can reveal wasted resources and cases where apparent cooperation does not improve welfare (Han et al., 2024).

The mechanisms behind these behaviours remain uncertain: our data show choices, not reasoning. One possibility is that an equal split acts as a focal point that models reconstruct even without an explicit hint (Dodivers and Rafai, 2025). Another is that questions prompt calculation while requests to act elicit a behavioural default (Fan et al., 2024; Schmied et al., 2026). Post-training may also encourage models to contribute their share unless instructed otherwise, consistent with findings that models are more cooperative than people (Mei et al., 2024) and that cooperation increases with the stakes in repeated prisoner’s dilemmas, contrary to evolutionary predictions (Huynh et al., 2026). Stronger reasoning is not necessarily a remedy: reasoning models can free-ride more in public-goods games (Guzman Piedrahita et al., 2025). These accounts are hypotheses, not explanations established by our experiments.

Limitations, scope, and reproducibility. The goal sentence is tested in only one phrasing and in self-play; without a group-payoff goal, we cannot distinguish the effect of making the objective explicit from the effect of the instruction’s direction. Because the running pool is not displayed, arithmetic errors may explain some contributions made after the group has already met its target. The value questions also omit p=0p=0.

We test five models, one from each provider, in English and in a single game. Our claims therefore concern this panel and setting, not language models in general. Ten games per condition limit statistical power, and a zero-width bootstrap interval for a constant sample should not be interpreted as evidence of deterministic behaviour. Our prompt rewordings cover only a small portion of the prompt space; welfare losses assume risk neutrality. The scripted, mixed, and selection designs use the base prompt. Fixed seat blocks confound player composition with position, and the selection analysis assumes rare entry.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
